What you will practice · Choose your pace

What you will practice

  • Replace an overstated development claim with a precise finding and a testable next question.
  • Frame a focused regulatory question and accurately record the scope of the response.
  • Resolve conflicting trial instructions through an explicit, documented clarification rather than choosing a convenient version.
  • Explain a trial readout without replacing the prespecified question or overstating statistical certainty.
  • Preserve reported facts, avoid premature causality judgments, and route a safety report without waiting for perfect information.

Choose your pace

Quick practice · 15 minutes: complete one short exchange, check the explanations, and read both roles aloud.

Extended practice · two or three sittings: check the case facts, study the vocabulary and phrases, complete the longer conversation, then rehearse the follow-up exchange.

Level guide: designed for intermediate to advanced learners. B1 learners can start with the short exchanges and supplied phrases; B2 learners can complete the cloze conversations; C1 learners can focus on the distinctions in the language checks. These are teaching suggestions, not a certified level assessment.

01Drug Development Strategy, Unmet Need, TPP, and Evidence LogicA laboratory signal becomes a patient-benefit claim+

Your goal

Replace an overstated development claim with a precise finding and a testable next question.

This lesson in the book, page 4 ↗

A Read the situation

A laboratory signal becomes a patient-benefit claim

An internal slide for fictional candidate PX-17 says it improves patient mobility. The available experiment used a cell-based assay, not patients. Across three experimental runs, the team observed a change in a disease-related marker at one tested concentration. Human exposure, tolerability, and clinical benefit have not been established. Scientist Leila and development lead Owen are preparing a portfolio discussion. The proposed target product profile describes a desired future benefit, not an achieved product characteristic. No clinical study is authorized by this discussion.

Leila: Translational scientist / Owen: Development lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. Where was the observed result obtained?

Answer and explanation

A. In a cell-based assay across three experimental runs

The supplied evidence is laboratory evidence, with no patient study or approved label in the case.

2. What does the target product profile represent here?

Answer and explanation

A. Desired future characteristics to guide development

The proposed profile sets aspirations; it does not establish that those characteristics have been demonstrated.

3. Which claim exceeds the evidence?

Answer and explanation

D. PX-17 improves patient mobility.

No patients were studied, so the laboratory result cannot establish a patient mobility benefit.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A biomarker change is not automatically clinical benefit. Its meaning depends on the marker, context, and supporting evidence. Here, one concentration and three laboratory runs do not establish human exposure, tolerability, dose response, or improved mobility.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
unmet medical need
A health-related need not adequately addressed by available options.characterize the unmet medical need
target product profile
A planning description of desired future product characteristics.refine the target product profile
development candidate
A selected investigational substance being evaluated for further development.nominate a development candidate
mechanism of action
The biological process through which an intervention produces an effect.investigate the mechanism of action
target engagement
Evidence that an intervention interacts with its intended biological target.assess target engagement
proof of concept
Evidence supporting the feasibility of a defined scientific or clinical idea.specify the proof-of-concept question
cell-based assay
A laboratory test using cells to assess a specified response.qualify the cell-based assay
biomarker
A measured characteristic indicating a biological process or response.evaluate a candidate biomarker
surrogate endpoint
A substitute outcome used to predict a clinical outcome, with context-dependent support.justify a surrogate endpoint
clinical benefit
A meaningful favorable effect on how patients feel, function, or survive.establish clinical benefit
translational evidence
Information connecting findings across experimental and human contexts.strengthen translational evidence
biological plausibility
A reasoned basis for believing a biological explanation could be credible.assess biological plausibility
dose-response relationship
How a measured effect varies with administered dose.characterize the dose-response relationship
exposure-response relationship
How an effect varies with drug exposure in the body.examine exposure-response relationships
pharmacokinetics
Study of the time course of drug exposure through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination.characterize pharmacokinetics
pharmacodynamics
Study of a drug's biological effects and their relation to exposure.measure pharmacodynamic effects
nonclinical study
Research conducted outside human clinical studies.interpret nonclinical findings
tolerability
The extent to which unwanted effects can be endured in a defined context.evaluate tolerability
therapeutic window
The exposure range associated with desired effects and acceptable toxicity in context.investigate the therapeutic window
repeatability
Agreement between repeated results under the same specified measurement conditions.assess repeatability
assay limitation
A restriction affecting what a test can establish.disclose assay limitations
go/no-go criterion
A defined condition informing whether development proceeds or stops.set go/no-go criteria
evidence gap
Missing information needed to support a proposed conclusion.prioritize evidence gaps
development milestone
A defined point of progress or review in a development program.plan the next development milestone

Target product profile is often shortened to TPP; mechanism of action to MOA; pharmacokinetics to PK; and pharmacodynamics to PD. Expand the terms when needed, and distinguish a planned characteristic from an observed result. A development goal must not silently become an evidence claim.

C Notice the language

A narrower claim can be more useful

Do not soften an unsupported assertion merely by adding promising. State what was measured, where it was measured, and what remains unknown. Then connect the result to the next question. This lets a colleague support further investigation without endorsing a conclusion the evidence cannot carry.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Locate the evidence
The observation comes from a cell-based assay, not a patient study.
Narrow the claim
We observed a marker change under the tested conditions.
Protect the distinction
Clinical benefit has not been established.
Clarify the aspiration
The target product profile describes what we aim to demonstrate.
Ask for the bridge
What evidence connects this marker to the intended patient outcome?
Qualify repetition
Three runs support repeatability within these conditions, not general clinical effectiveness.
Name the limitation
We tested one concentration, so this does not characterize a dose-response relationship.
State the next question
We need to test whether the finding persists under relevant follow-up conditions.
Avoid implied safety
The current experiment does not establish human tolerability.
Check the population
Which patients would the proposed product eventually be intended to serve?
Separate stages
An early signal supports investigation, not a treatment recommendation.
Request a criterion
What result would support the next development decision?
Clarify the measure
Are we discussing target engagement, a biomarker, or a patient outcome?
Keep the goal conditional
The desired benefit remains a hypothesis to be evaluated.
Mark authority
This portfolio discussion does not authorize a clinical study.
Close accurately
Retain the finding, its conditions, and the unresolved evidence gap.
6 language and precision notes
Observed
Use for the measured result, not for an extrapolated patient benefit.
Suggests
State exactly what the result suggests and why.
Proof of concept
Specify the concept; laboratory and clinical proof are different claims.
TPP
This is a planning tool, not automatically an approved label.
At one concentration
This qualifier limits what can be said about response across concentrations.
In patients
Do not add this phrase when the evidence comes only from laboratory work.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which replacement is best supported?

Answer and explanation

C. PX-17 changed the marker in the tested cell assay; patient benefit remains unestablished.

The replacement preserves the observed laboratory finding while explicitly limiting the clinical inference.

2. What does testing one concentration fail to characterize?

Answer and explanation

A. How the effect changes across different concentrations

A response across concentrations requires additional concentration conditions; the supplied experiment used only one.

3. Which additional question most directly tests the proposed marker-to-mobility claim?

Answer and explanation

A. What evidence links changes in this marker to patient mobility in the intended context?

The missing bridge is evidence connecting the measured marker with the intended patient outcome. Repetition, an added population label, and a planning aspiration do not establish that connection.

4. What can the portfolio discussion decide on the supplied authority?

Answer and explanation

C. A proposed next investigation for appropriate review, not automatic clinical-study authorization

The brief excludes clinical-study authorization and supplies no basis for treatment or marketing claims.

E Conversations

A laboratory signal becomes a patient-benefit claim

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Leila: Translational scientist / Owen: Development lead

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

Word bank
  • dose-response relationship
  • biomarker
  • tolerability
  • development milestone
  • go/no-go criterion
  • clinical benefit
  • cell-based assay
  • evidence gap
  • repeatability
  • target product profile
  1. Owen
    The portfolio slide says PX-17 improves patient mobility. I thought the latest package contained laboratory work only. Have I missed a clinical result?
  2. Leila
    No. The result comes from a 1. We saw the marker change across three runs at one tested concentration. Nobody measured mobility in patients.
  3. Owen
    Then the headline has moved beyond the evidence. The team wanted a clear link to the disease, but the wording makes that link sound demonstrated.
  4. Leila
    We can describe the 2 response precisely and explain why it interests us. We still need evidence connecting that response to the outcome we hope to influence.
  5. Owen
    The commercial planning page also lists improved mobility. That is in the target profile, so perhaps someone copied it into the result summary.
  6. Leila
    The 3 is aspirational at this stage. We should label the desired outcome separately from the finding so readers do not confuse the development goal with achieved performance.
  7. Owen
    Can we call this proof of concept? The phrase is familiar, but different colleagues may hear very different claims when they read it.
  8. Leila
    Specify the concept and setting. It is not evidence of 4. A broad proof-of-concept label could conceal exactly the distinction we are trying to restore.
  9. Owen
    Why is there a rising dose-response arrow if we tested only one concentration? The graphic seems to be claiming something the experiment did not measure.
  10. Leila
    Remove that implication. A 5 has not been characterized here. The visual should not make a stronger statement than the accompanying words or the experiment itself.
  11. Owen
    What can we say about the three runs? I do not want to discard useful repetition merely because the result is still early.
  12. Leila
    The runs used the same analyst, method, and equipment over a short interval. They inform 6. Show all three results and their variation, not just the strongest one.
  13. Owen
    Someone has added well tolerated to the summary. There were no human participants, so I cannot see what that statement is based on.
  14. Leila
    Human 7 is unestablished. We can report the actual observations, but we should not translate the absence of a particular laboratory finding into a general human safety claim.
  15. Owen
    Let us make the next decision concrete. What missing information matters most before the program can support a stronger development proposal?
  16. Leila
    Start with the 8 between the assay response and the intended outcome. The scientific team should define the follow-up question and its limits through the appropriate development process.
  17. Owen
    The committee will ask what would count as enough progress to continue. A broad instruction to produce more data will not help them compare programs.
  18. Leila
    Propose a defined 9 for qualified review. It should match the next decision, without pretending that an early laboratory threshold alone establishes a product suitable for patients.
  19. Owen
    I will replace the mobility headline with the assay finding. Send me the limits and proposed next question so the committee sees what this result supports.
  20. Leila
    Good. The next 10 remains subject to the required review. This discussion does not authorize a clinical study, and the final slide should say no more than the evidence supports.

Answers and explanations
  1. cell-based assay Turn 2. A cell-based assay is laboratory evidence, not a study establishing outcomes in patients.
  2. biomarker Turn 4. The biomarker is the measured biological characteristic; its change does not itself establish improved patient function.
  3. target product profile Turn 6. The target product profile sets desired future characteristics rather than recording benefits already demonstrated.
  4. clinical benefit Turn 8. Clinical benefit concerns meaningful patient outcomes; this experiment did not measure any patient outcome.
  5. dose-response relationship Turn 10. Dose-response describes effects across doses; the single tested concentration cannot establish that relationship.
  6. repeatability Turn 12. Repeatability concerns agreement under the same specified measurement conditions; it does not establish performance across laboratories or in patients.
  7. tolerability Turn 14. Tolerability concerns enduring unwanted effects in a defined context; this laboratory experiment did not establish human tolerability.
  8. evidence gap Turn 16. The evidence gap is missing information connecting the assay finding to a more meaningful development conclusion.
  9. go/no-go criterion Turn 18. A go/no-go criterion identifies evidence needed for a development decision rather than treating all additional data as progress.
  10. development milestone Turn 20. A development milestone is a defined progress or review point, not automatic authorization for human studies.
Read the complete conversation
  1. Owen: The portfolio slide says PX-17 improves patient mobility. I thought the latest package contained laboratory work only. Have I missed a clinical result?
  2. Leila: No. The result comes from a cell-based assay. We saw the marker change across three runs at one tested concentration. Nobody measured mobility in patients.
  3. Owen: Then the headline has moved beyond the evidence. The team wanted a clear link to the disease, but the wording makes that link sound demonstrated.
  4. Leila: We can describe the biomarker response precisely and explain why it interests us. We still need evidence connecting that response to the outcome we hope to influence.
  5. Owen: The commercial planning page also lists improved mobility. That is in the target profile, so perhaps someone copied it into the result summary.
  6. Leila: The target product profile is aspirational at this stage. We should label the desired outcome separately from the finding so readers do not confuse the development goal with achieved performance.
  7. Owen: Can we call this proof of concept? The phrase is familiar, but different colleagues may hear very different claims when they read it.
  8. Leila: Specify the concept and setting. It is not evidence of clinical benefit. A broad proof-of-concept label could conceal exactly the distinction we are trying to restore.
  9. Owen: Why is there a rising dose-response arrow if we tested only one concentration? The graphic seems to be claiming something the experiment did not measure.
  10. Leila: Remove that implication. A dose-response relationship has not been characterized here. The visual should not make a stronger statement than the accompanying words or the experiment itself.
  11. Owen: What can we say about the three runs? I do not want to discard useful repetition merely because the result is still early.
  12. Leila: The runs used the same analyst, method, and equipment over a short interval. They inform repeatability. Show all three results and their variation, not just the strongest one.
  13. Owen: Someone has added well tolerated to the summary. There were no human participants, so I cannot see what that statement is based on.
  14. Leila: Human tolerability is unestablished. We can report the actual observations, but we should not translate the absence of a particular laboratory finding into a general human safety claim.
  15. Owen: Let us make the next decision concrete. What missing information matters most before the program can support a stronger development proposal?

  18. Leila: Propose a defined go/no-go criterion for qualified review. It should match the next decision, without pretending that an early laboratory threshold alone establishes a product suitable for patients.

Dialogue in the book, page 10 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

A laboratory signal is not patient benefit

Fictional development-slide review: a laboratory result is promising, but no clinical benefit has been established.

  1. Development lead: This slide says our candidate will benefit patients. What evidence supports that wording?
  2. Research scientist: We observed the intended response in the laboratory system, not in patients.
  3. Development lead: Could we describe that as confirmation of the proposed mechanism of action, or MOA?
  4. Research scientist: That is still too strong. The result supports our hypothesis under these experimental conditions.
  5. Development lead: Then how should we connect it to the target product profile, the TPP?
  6. Research scientist: Present the TPP as a development target, with clinical benefit listed as unestablished.
  7. Development lead: Should the indication remain on the slide as the proposed patient population?
  8. Research scientist: Yes, provided we label it proposed and avoid implying an approved use.
  9. Development lead: I'll replace the benefit claim and separate evidence from the development objective.
  10. Research scientist: I'll check that the laboratory conditions and remaining evidence gaps stay visible.
Two indications, one evidence package

Separate fictional portfolio discussion: candidate P7 has laboratory data for indication A; indication B has only a biological rationale.

  1. Portfolio manager: Can we put indications A and B at the same development stage?
  2. Translational scientist: Not on this evidence. P7 has laboratory data for A and a rationale for B.
  3. Portfolio manager: The proposed MOA is similar. Doesn't that support the same conclusion for both?
  4. Translational scientist: It supports asking the question, not assuming that the results will transfer.
  5. Portfolio manager: How do we explain the difference without making B sound irrelevant?
  6. Translational scientist: Call B an exploratory opportunity and identify the experiment needed to assess it.
  7. Portfolio manager: Would a separate TPP make that distinction clearer for the committee?
  8. Translational scientist: Possibly, but its targets must not appear to be measured product characteristics.
  9. Portfolio manager: I'll show observed evidence for A beside the unanswered questions for B.
  10. Translational scientist: Good. The committee can discuss priorities without confusing potential with demonstrated performance.
Readiness for discussion versus readiness for filing

Separate fictional project check-in: an IND planning discussion is scheduled, but the supporting evidence inventory is incomplete.

  1. Project manager: The calendar says IND readiness. Can I report that the package is ready?
  2. Regulatory scientist: No. That is the meeting topic; our evidence inventory is still incomplete.
  3. Project manager: I understood the title to mean an investigational new drug submission was imminent.
  4. Regulatory scientist: We're reviewing gaps before proposing a filing schedule, not confirming a submission date.
  5. Project manager: Which part of the update can I state with confidence today?
  6. Regulatory scientist: The planning discussion is scheduled. The package assessment and timing remain open.
  7. Project manager: Should I include the proposed indication and TPP in that discussion?
  8. Regulatory scientist: Yes. They explain what we intend to develop and why particular evidence matters.
  9. Project manager: I'll correct the milestone wording and avoid treating a meeting as a completed assessment.
  10. Regulatory scientist: I'll bring the inventory and clearly distinguish available documents from expected ones.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A laboratory signal becomes a patient-benefit claim
  1. Check the cloze key and read the PX-17 discussion. Emphasize cell-based assay, one concentration, and three runs without adding patient results.
  2. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Distinguish repeatability under the stated conditions from human tolerability and the desired mobility benefit.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

A goal is not a result

A planning profile targets once-daily use. The candidate has no human dosing data. A laboratory test measured target engagement but did not measure patient symptoms.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Scientist: "Once-daily use is currently a ___."

Answer and explanation

D. goal

The planning profile states an intended characteristic, while no human dosing evidence is supplied.

2. Reviewer: "The measured laboratory finding concerns ___."

Answer and explanation

B. target engagement

The test measured interaction with the intended target, not patient symptoms.

3. Scientist: "Human dosing remains ___."

Answer and explanation

A. unestablished

The brief explicitly says there are no human dosing data.

4. Reviewer: "We cannot claim symptom ___."

Answer and explanation

B. improvement

Patient symptoms were not measured, so an improvement claim would exceed the evidence.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Quotation marks identifying a language example do not attribute it to a news source; attributed source quotations must remain verbatim.

Practice setting: B2 independent. Use natural professional English with brief explanations. Let me attempt each task without a model first. Offer a hint after difficulty and invite a more precise retry.

TASK: Choose grammar that preserves the meaning
1. Use the lesson's language workshop, or one actual sentence from the dialogue, to explain a single grammar distinction in no more than 90 words. Show how it affects timing, certainty, responsibility or politeness.
2. Give one brief occupational exchange containing a gap and four complete options A-D. Supply enough context for exactly one answer. Keep distractors plausible; distinguish grammar errors from wording that changes the facts. Stop and wait.
3. Explain why each choice fits or fails, then ask me to read the completed exchange aloud. Do not request a draft, original written sentence or essay.
4. Repeat with three new exchanges, one at a time, moving from recognition to a more subtle meaning contrast. Do not copy the published checks. Label invented variations and do not turn uncertainty into a promise.
5. End with a short contrast table and two supported spoken turns using supplied frames. Accept accurate alternatives in oral practice; acknowledge and replace ambiguous multiple-choice items.

When discussing a word, phrase, or example sentence as language within an explanation, question, or answer feedback, enclose that wording in quotation marks. For example: What does “about” mean in “about twenty people”? Use “on” with a named day. Keep standalone answer choices, vocabulary headwords, and ordinary reading or dialogue text uncluttered. Course: Pharmaceutical English
Professional audience: clinical development, regulatory affairs, pharmacovigilance, quality, CMC, manufacturing, medical affairs, market access, and compliance teams
Scope: Original fictional language practice, not medical advice, clinical training, regulatory guidance, or authorization to perform regulated work. US terminology is used where identified; requirements vary by jurisdiction, product, and context. Follow current approved procedures, qualified professional judgment, and applicable requirements.
Lesson 01: Drug Development Strategy, Unmet Need, TPP, and Evidence Logic
Original fictional case: An internal slide for fictional candidate PX-17 says it improves patient mobility. The available experiment used a cell-based assay, not patients. Across three experimental runs, the team observed a change in a disease-related marker at one tested concentration. Human exposure, tolerability, and clinical benefit have not been established. Scientist Leila and development lead Owen are preparing a portfolio discussion. The proposed target product profile describes a desired future benefit, not an achieved product characteristic. No clinical study is authorized by this discussion.
Language workshop: A laboratory signal becomes a patient-benefit claim
Communication goal: Replace an overstated development claim with a precise finding and a testable next question.
Language guidance: A biomarker change is not automatically clinical benefit. Its meaning depends on the marker, context, and supporting evidence. Here, one concentration and three laboratory runs do not establish human exposure, tolerability, dose response, or improved mobility.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The observation comes from a cell-based assay, not a patient study. / We observed a marker change under the tested conditions. / Clinical benefit has not been established. / The target product profile describes what we aim to demonstrate. / What evidence connects this marker to the intended patient outcome? / Three runs support repeatability within these conditions, not general clinical effectiveness. / We tested one concentration, so this does not characterize a dose-response relationship. / We need to test whether the finding persists under relevant follow-up conditions. / The current experiment does not establish human tolerability. / Which patients would the proposed product eventually be intended to serve? / An early signal supports investigation, not a treatment recommendation. / What result would support the next development decision? / Are we discussing target engagement, a biomarker, or a patient outcome? / The desired benefit remains a hypothesis to be evaluated. / This portfolio discussion does not authorize a clinical study. / Retain the finding, its conditions, and the unresolved evidence gap.
Vocabulary: unmet medical need: A health-related need not adequately addressed by available options. / target product profile: A planning description of desired future product characteristics. / development candidate: A selected investigational substance being evaluated for further development. / mechanism of action: The biological process through which an intervention produces an effect. / target engagement: Evidence that an intervention interacts with its intended biological target. / proof of concept: Evidence supporting the feasibility of a defined scientific or clinical idea. / cell-based assay: A laboratory test using cells to assess a specified response. / biomarker: A measured characteristic indicating a biological process or response. / surrogate endpoint: A substitute outcome used to predict a clinical outcome, with context-dependent support. / clinical benefit: A meaningful favorable effect on how patients feel, function, or survive. / translational evidence: Information connecting findings across experimental and human contexts. / biological plausibility: A reasoned basis for believing a biological explanation could be credible. / dose-response relationship: How a measured effect varies with administered dose. / exposure-response relationship: How an effect varies with drug exposure in the body. / pharmacokinetics: Study of the time course of drug exposure through absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination. / pharmacodynamics: Study of a drug's biological effects and their relation to exposure. / nonclinical study: Research conducted outside human clinical studies. / tolerability: The extent to which unwanted effects can be endured in a defined context. / therapeutic window: The exposure range associated with desired effects and acceptable toxicity in context. / repeatability: Agreement between repeated results under the same specified measurement conditions. / assay limitation: A restriction affecting what a test can establish. / go/no-go criterion: A defined condition informing whether development proceeds or stops. / evidence gap: Missing information needed to support a proposed conclusion. / development milestone: A defined point of progress or review in a development program.
Speaking task: Check the cloze key and read the PX-17 discussion. Emphasize cell-based assay, one concentration, and three runs without adding patient results. Switch roles for turns 11-20. Distinguish repeatability under the stated conditions from human tolerability and the desired mobility benefit. Complete and check the planning-profile exchange. Read once-daily use as a goal, target engagement as the observed finding, and human dosing as unestablished.
Partner: Leila: Translational scientist / Owen: Development lead
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A planning profile targets once-daily use. The candidate has no human dosing data. A laboratory test measured target engagement but did not measure patient symptoms.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Owen: The committee will ask what would count as enough progress to continue. A broad instruction to produce more data will not help them compare programs.
Leila: Propose a defined go/no-go criterion for qualified review. It should match the next decision, without pretending that an early laboratory threshold alone establishes a product suitable for patients.
Owen: I will replace the mobility headline with the assay finding. Send me the limits and proposed next question so the committee sees what this result supports.
Leila: Good. The next development milestone remains subject to the required review. This discussion does not authorize a clinical study, and the final slide should say no more than the evidence supports.
END REFERENCE
Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

02Regulatory Pathways, IND Readiness, NDA/BLA Strategy, and Agency InteractionA meeting question that asks for blanket agreement+

Your goal

Frame a focused regulatory question and accurately record the scope of the response.

This lesson in the book, page 13 ↗

A Read the situation

A meeting question that asks for blanket agreement

A US development team is preparing an agency meeting package for fictional investigational product RV-8. Its draft asks whether the entire development plan is acceptable. The immediate unresolved question concerns the proposed patient population and the rationale for a planned study endpoint. Supporting summaries exist, but two supporting reports are unfinished. Regulatory lead Priya and clinical lead Evan must distinguish the sponsor proposal, available evidence, and specific advice requested. No agency response has been received, and meeting preparation does not constitute authorization to begin the study.

Priya: Regulatory lead / Evan: Clinical lead

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is wrong with the current question?

Answer and explanation

C. It asks broadly about the entire plan instead of the specific unresolved proposal.

The real issue concerns population and endpoint rationale, while the draft requests undifferentiated agreement with the entire plan.

2. What is the status of two supporting reports?

Answer and explanation

B. Unfinished

The brief explicitly says two supporting reports remain unfinished.

3. Which statement is accurate now?

Answer and explanation

B. No agency response has been received.

Preparation is ongoing, and the case supplies no response or study authorization.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

IND means investigational new drug application; NDA means new drug application; BLA means biologics license application in US usage. These terms name different regulatory submissions. An IND is not a marketing approval, and preparing a meeting package does not authorize a study.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
regulatory strategy
A plan for addressing applicable regulatory requirements and interactions.align the regulatory strategy
regulatory pathway
The applicable route for development, review, or authorization.confirm the regulatory pathway
investigational new drug application
A US submission supporting proposed clinical investigation of a drug.prepare an IND submission
new drug application
A US application seeking approval to market a new drug.plan the NDA content
biologics license application
A US application seeking licensure of a biological product.prepare the BLA strategy
agency interaction
A formal or informal exchange with a regulatory authority.document the agency interaction
meeting package
Materials submitted to support a scheduled regulatory discussion.assemble the meeting package
briefing document
A structured account of background, evidence, proposals, and questions.finalize the briefing document
sponsor position
The development sponsor's proposed approach and rationale.state the sponsor position
focused question
A question limited to a defined issue that can receive a useful answer.formulate a focused question
supporting rationale
The reasoning and evidence behind a proposal.substantiate the supporting rationale
information gap
Missing material relevant to assessing a proposal.disclose an information gap
submission readiness
The state of being sufficiently prepared for an intended submission.assess submission readiness
dossier
An organized collection of documents supporting regulatory review.maintain a coherent dossier
cross-reference
A pointer connecting a statement to supporting material.verify the cross-reference
version control
Management of document revisions and their status.maintain version control
regulatory commitment
An undertaking made in the relevant regulatory context.track regulatory commitments
meeting minutes
The documented account of a meeting's discussion and outcomes.reconcile meeting minutes
written response
A documented reply to a submitted question or issue.review the written response
conditional advice
Advice whose applicability depends on stated circumstances.preserve conditional advice
clinical hold
A regulatory order delaying or suspending a clinical investigation in the US context.address a clinical hold
approval status
The actual state of a specified authorization decision.verify approval status
indication
The disease, condition, or use for which a product is intended or authorized in context.define the proposed indication
regulatory affairs
The function coordinating regulatory strategy, submissions, and interactions.consult regulatory affairs

Agency advice may address a specific question under stated assumptions. Preserve those limits in the meeting record. Do not report advice on a population or endpoint as approval of the complete program, final labeling, or a marketing application.

C Notice the language

Make the question answerable

A focused question gives reviewers a proposal, supporting rationale, and a specific point on which advice is sought. Avoid treating a useful discussion as blanket agreement with every part of a program. Meeting records should preserve conditions, unresolved issues, and any distinction between advice and formal authorization.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
Focus the question
We seek advice on the proposed population and endpoint rationale.
State the sponsor view
Our proposed approach is set out in section three.
Supply the reason
The rationale rests on the following evidence and assumptions.
Disclose incompleteness
Two supporting reports are not yet final.
Avoid blanket agreement
This question does not ask for approval of the entire program.
Check the reference
Please verify that the cited section supports this statement.
Distinguish status
The package is in preparation; no agency response has been received.
Preserve a condition
Record the qualification alongside the advice, not in a separate summary.
Confirm the pathway
Regulatory affairs should confirm the applicable route for this product.
Separate submissions
An IND and a marketing application serve different purposes.
Resolve a discrepancy
The summary and supporting report currently describe different populations.
Control the version
Use the agreed document version for the submitted package.
Track an undertaking
Identify the owner and due date for each recorded commitment.
Limit the conclusion
Advice on this question does not settle every development issue.
Mark study authority
Meeting preparation is not permission to begin the study.
Close the record
Distinguish answered questions, conditions, and issues still open.
6 language and precision notes
Acceptable in what respect
Ask which specific proposal and evidence the question concerns.
Sponsor position
This is the company's proposal, not the authority's conclusion.
Final versus available
A draft can be available without being final or approved.
Advice versus authorization
Keep the applicable legal and procedural status explicit.
No objection
Do not paraphrase a limited response as unrestricted approval.
As proposed
This phrase ties the response to the details actually presented.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which agency question is focused on the immediate unresolved proposal?

Answer and explanation

C. Does the proposed population and endpoint rationale in section three address the intended study objective?

The focused question identifies the population, endpoint rationale, supporting section, and study objective. It does not seek blanket endorsement, alter document status, or imply a future marketing decision.

2. Which package statement is accurate?

Answer and explanation

D. Two reports remain unfinished and their status is identified.

The statement preserves the actual document status and allows reviewers to understand the information gap.

3. Which distinction is correct in US terminology?

Answer and explanation

D. An IND supports clinical investigation; an NDA seeks marketing approval for a new drug.

These submissions serve different purposes, and permission or advice at one stage does not guarantee later approval.

4. How should limited advice be summarized?

Answer and explanation

D. Preserve its subject, assumptions, conditions, and unresolved issues.

An accurate record retains the boundaries of the actual response instead of changing its meaning.

Answers and explanations
  1. focused question Turn 2. A focused question identifies the specific unresolved issue, here population and endpoint rationale.
  2. sponsor position Turn 4. The sponsor position is the company's proposed approach, which must not be confused with agency agreement.
  3. information gap Turn 6. The information gap is the unfinished supporting material, whose status must remain visible in the package.
  4. briefing document Turn 8. The briefing document should present a coherent proposal, evidence, and questions rather than conflicting population descriptions.
  5. cross-reference Turn 10. A cross-reference must lead to material that actually supports the statement, including after document revisions.
  6. investigational new drug application Turn 12. An investigational new drug application concerns clinical investigation in the US; a meeting package is not itself that authorization.
  7. regulatory pathway Turn 14. The regulatory pathway is the applicable route for this product, which qualified regulatory colleagues must confirm.
  8. conditional advice Turn 16. Conditional advice applies within stated circumstances; removing those conditions changes the meaning of the response.
  9. meeting minutes Turn 18. Meeting minutes record the discussion and outcomes; discrepancies should be resolved through the applicable process.
  10. approval status Turn 20. Approval status must reflect the actual authorization record, not expectations created by meeting preparation or positive discussion.

Dialogue in the book, page 19 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

A regulatory question the team can actually discuss

Fictional preparation for an agency meeting: the draft question asks whether the entire development plan is acceptable.

  1. Regulatory lead: Our question asks whether the whole plan is acceptable. What specific feedback do we need?
  2. Clinical lead: We need feedback on the proposed evidence supporting the next development stage.
  3. Regulatory lead: That still covers several topics. Which uncertainty affects our immediate planning decision?
  4. Clinical lead: Whether our proposed study population addresses the question described in the briefing document.
  5. Regulatory lead: Then let's ask about that population and provide our rationale, rather than request blanket approval.
  6. Clinical lead: Should we mention the IND in the opening sentence for context?
  7. Regulatory lead: Yes, but distinguish our current planning question from any future submission outcome.
  8. Clinical lead: I'll revise the question and identify the relevant briefing section this afternoon.
  9. Regulatory lead: Please send it for internal review before we finalize the meeting materials.
  10. Clinical lead: Understood. I'll request focused feedback without suggesting that a discussion guarantees acceptance.
Confirming which submission label belongs in the plan

Separate fictional planning meeting: a slide lists NDA/BLA as interchangeable placeholders; the regulatory strategy has not been confirmed.

  1. Program manager: Can you select NDA or BLA so our timeline looks complete?
  2. Regulatory strategist: I can review the terminology, but I shouldn't choose a route for appearance.
  3. Program manager: What information do you need from the technical team to assess it?
  4. Regulatory strategist: Please provide the current product description and the assumptions behind the proposed submission strategy.
  5. Program manager: Could we call both labels equivalent until that review is finished?
  6. Regulatory strategist: No. A new drug application and a biologics license application are distinct submission terms.
  7. Program manager: I'll mark the route as under review. Can you assess the description before Thursday's planning session?
  8. Regulatory strategist: I can give an initial assessment then, with unresolved questions clearly identified.
  9. Program manager: That will let us discuss dependencies without presenting an invented regulatory conclusion.
  10. Regulatory strategist: Agreed. I'll also specify what further specialist review is needed before the label is finalized.
Assigning questions after a response letter

Separate fictional internal exercise: a complete response letter lists three issues, and the team has not yet assigned reviewers.

  1. Regulatory coordinator: We have three issues in the complete response letter and no assigned reviewers yet.
  2. Program lead: Can we tell the board that resolving those issues guarantees approval?
  3. Regulatory coordinator: No. We can describe our response planning, not promise the outcome of another review.
  4. Program lead: What action do you need from me before tomorrow's internal meeting?
  5. Regulatory coordinator: Please nominate an accountable reviewer for each issue and confirm their availability.
  6. Program lead: Should those reviewers commit to completion dates immediately, before assessing the requested work?
  7. Regulatory coordinator: Ask for initial scope estimates first. Some dependencies may still be unknown.
  8. Program lead: I'll request owners today and ask them to identify unanswered questions tomorrow.
  9. Regulatory coordinator: I'll keep each response item linked to the relevant wording in the letter.
  10. Program lead: Then our update can distinguish assigned work, estimated timing, and decisions we cannot predict.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

A meeting question that asks for blanket agreement
  1. Check the answers, then read the RV-8 meeting-preparation exchange. Keep the population and endpoint question distinct from approval of the whole program.
  2. Switch roles for the document discussion. Preserve the two unfinished reports and the absence of any agency response or study authorization.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

The response answers one question

An invented meeting note supports an endpoint approach only for the population described in the package. It requests further justification of follow-up duration. It grants no marketing authorization.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Regulatory lead: "The endpoint advice is ___."

Answer and explanation

D. conditional

The note limits support to the population actually described, so it is not unconditional agreement.

2. Clinical lead: "Follow-up duration remains ___."

Answer and explanation

C. unresolved

Further justification is requested, so the note does not settle that issue.

3. Regulatory lead: "Preserve the stated ___."

Answer and explanation

B. population

The population defines the scope within which the endpoint advice applies.

4. Clinical lead: "This is not marketing ___."

Answer and explanation

A. authorization

The briefing explicitly excludes marketing authorization, regardless of the favorable endpoint comment.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Vocabulary: regulatory strategy: A plan for addressing applicable regulatory requirements and interactions. / regulatory pathway: The applicable route for development, review, or authorization. / investigational new drug application: A US submission supporting proposed clinical investigation of a drug. / new drug application: A US application seeking approval to market a new drug. / biologics license application: A US application seeking licensure of a biological product. / agency interaction: A formal or informal exchange with a regulatory authority. / meeting package: Materials submitted to support a scheduled regulatory discussion. / briefing document: A structured account of background, evidence, proposals, and questions. / sponsor position: The development sponsor's proposed approach and rationale. / focused question: A question limited to a defined issue that can receive a useful answer. / supporting rationale: The reasoning and evidence behind a proposal. / information gap: Missing material relevant to assessing a proposal. / submission readiness: The state of being sufficiently prepared for an intended submission. / dossier: An organized collection of documents supporting regulatory review. / cross-reference: A pointer connecting a statement to supporting material. / version control: Management of document revisions and their status. / regulatory commitment: An undertaking made in the relevant regulatory context. / meeting minutes: The documented account of a meeting's discussion and outcomes. / written response: A documented reply to a submitted question or issue. / conditional advice: Advice whose applicability depends on stated circumstances. / clinical hold: A regulatory order delaying or suspending a clinical investigation in the US context. / approval status: The actual state of a specified authorization decision. / indication: The disease, condition, or use for which a product is intended or authorized in context. / regulatory affairs: The function coordinating regulatory strategy, submissions, and interactions.

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.

03Clinical Trial Design, Protocols, GCP, and OperationsTwo visit windows and no confirmed controlling version+

Your goal

Resolve conflicting trial instructions through an explicit, documented clarification rather than choosing a convenient version.

This lesson in the book, page 22 ↗

A Read the situation

Two visit windows and no confirmed controlling version

Coordinator Maya is scheduling next week. A protocol attachment gives a plus-or-minus-three-day visit window; a site quick-reference sheet gives seven. The controlling version and site implementation status are unconfirmed. No participant awaits an urgent care decision. Clinical research associate Ben must obtain clarification through the investigator and sponsor process. Neither may invent a window, silently change records, or assume the newest attachment governs the site.

Maya: Site coordinator / Ben: Clinical research associate

Check the facts · 3 questions

Choose the answer supported by the briefing. Do not assume that a proposed action has already happened.

1. What is the documented conflict?

Answer and explanation

D. Three-day versus seven-day visit windows in two sources

The brief supplies conflicting window descriptions and no confirmed controlling version.

2. What has not been confirmed?

Answer and explanation

C. The controlling version and its implementation status at the site

Both document authority and site applicability remain unresolved in the supplied facts.

3. Which response avoids an unauthorized assumption?

Answer and explanation

B. Escalate the exact discrepancy for documented clarification through the applicable process.

The case requires authorized clarification, not a convenient choice, inferred authority, or silent alteration of records.

B Find the words

Vocabulary and collocations

A later file date does not establish that a document is approved and effective for a particular site. Confirm identity, version, authorization, and applicability. A quick-reference sheet should not silently replace the controlling protocol or become an unofficial amendment.

24 field terms and natural word combinations
protocol
The document specifying a clinical study's objectives, design, and procedures.follow the applicable protocol
protocol amendment
A documented change to a study protocol.implement an authorized protocol amendment
visit window
The allowed timing range for a specified study visit or assessment.confirm the visit window
schedule of assessments
The planned timing of study procedures and measurements.reconcile the schedule of assessments
controlling version
The authorized document version applicable to the work in question.identify the controlling version
effective date
The date from which a document or change applies in context.verify the effective date
site activation
Confirmation that a site meets the applicable conditions to begin specified study activity.confirm site activation status
principal investigator
The investigator responsible for leading the study at a site.consult the principal investigator
clinical research associate
A professional supporting study oversight and monitoring within assigned responsibilities.contact the clinical research associate
study coordinator
A site professional coordinating assigned trial activities.brief the study coordinator
good clinical practice
Principles and standards for ethical, reliable clinical trial conduct.apply good clinical practice
informed consent
The voluntary agreement process based on adequate study information and understanding.document the informed-consent process
institutional review board
A body reviewing research involving human participants in the US context.confirm institutional review board review
eligibility criterion
A condition determining whether someone may enter a study.verify eligibility criteria
randomization
Allocation to study groups using a chance-based method.protect the randomization process
blinding
Concealment of treatment allocation from specified parties.maintain blinding
source record
The original record or certified copy containing relevant study observations.preserve the source record
electronic case report form
An electronic tool for collecting protocol-required participant data.complete the electronic case report form
data query
A documented request to clarify or resolve a data issue.resolve a data query
protocol deviation
A departure from the study protocol.assess a potential protocol deviation
monitoring finding
An issue identified during study monitoring.document a monitoring finding
audit trail
A traceable record of changes and associated information.preserve the audit trail
training record
Documentation of completed instruction or qualification.verify the training record
essential record
A record supporting evaluation of trial conduct and result reliability.maintain essential records

GCP means good clinical practice; CRA, clinical research associate; PI, principal investigator; IRB, institutional review board; and eCRF, electronic case report form. Roles and approval processes vary. These exercises practice clarification, not instructions to alter care, consent, or study procedures.

C Notice the language

Read back the conflict exactly

A useful escalation states both wordings, identifies their sources, and asks a specific question about the applicable version. Avoid describing the issue merely as confusion at the site. Precise language helps colleagues resolve the document problem without assigning blame or improvising clinical instructions.

16 useful phrases, grouped by purpose
State the discrepancy
The protocol attachment says three days; the quick-reference sheet says seven.
Request the authority
Which approved version is effective for this site?
Identify the source
I will include the document identifiers and exact sections.
Avoid a guess
I cannot confirm the visit window from these conflicting files.
Escalate precisely
Please resolve the timing discrepancy through the investigator and sponsor process.
Protect the record
We must preserve the original entry and any documented correction history.
Separate status
Received by email does not necessarily mean approved for implementation.
Check training
Has the relevant site team completed the required update?
Limit the response
I am confirming the governing instruction, not proposing a new window.
Close the loop
Please acknowledge the clarification and identify any affected appointments.
Assess impact
After confirmation, determine whether any completed visits require review.
Avoid blame
The two sources conflict; let us establish the applicable instruction.
Keep care distinct
Administrative clarification must not replace appropriate clinical judgment.
Document the outcome
Record the confirmed version, effective status, and source of clarification.
Control obsolete copies
Handle superseded quick-reference material through the document process.
Confirm understanding
Please read back the confirmed window and the document it comes from.
6 language and precision notes
Applicable
A document can be approved but not yet applicable to a given site or activity.
Clarification versus amendment
Explaining an existing requirement differs from changing it.
Received versus implemented
Receipt of a file does not prove authorized implementation or training.
Source versus eCRF
These records have related but distinct roles; discrepancies need traceable resolution.
Potential deviation
Do not classify the event definitively before the governing facts are established.
Read-back
Repeat the key instruction and source to expose misunderstanding before action.

D Check your understanding

Choose the precise message

Choose one best answer using the case facts and the stated purpose.

1. Which message best resolves the three-day versus seven-day discrepancy?

Answer and explanation

B. Please identify the approved site-effective protocol version and section governing this visit window.

The governing version and site applicability are missing. Neither recency, scheduling convenience, nor an invented midpoint identifies the actual approved requirement.

2. What does a newer file date prove by itself?

Answer and explanation

C. Only that the file carries a later date, not that it governs the site

File recency alone does not establish approval, effective status, training, or authority to change records.

3. How should a necessary record correction be handled?

Answer and explanation

A. Through the applicable traceable correction process, preserving the original history

Traceable correction preserves what was recorded and why it changed, instead of concealing the original entry.

4. What should follow an authorized clarification?

Answer and explanation

C. Confirm understanding and assess affected appointments or records through the appropriate process.

The clarified instruction must reach the relevant people, and any impact needs assessment rather than an unsupported conclusion.

Check explanations in the book, page 89 ↗

Two visit windows and no confirmed controlling version

Extended conversation · 20 turns · 10 gaps

Maya: Site coordinator / Ben: Clinical research associate

Complete the numbered gaps. Use each bank entry once, without changing its form.

  1. Maya
    I am scheduling next week's visits and have two different windows. The protocol attachment says plus or minus three days; the quick-reference sheet says seven.
  2. Ben
    Please send the identifiers and exact sections for both. We need the 1 before confirming the schedule. I cannot choose a window from the filenames alone.
  3. Maya
    The seven-day sheet arrived in a newer email. The coordinator who forwarded it assumed that made it the current instruction for every site.
  4. Ben

Answers and explanations
  1. controlling version Turn 2. The controlling version is the authorized document applicable to this site, not whichever file is easier to use.
  2. effective date Turn 4. The effective date establishes when a document applies; a later email alone does not establish implementation status.
  3. schedule of assessments Turn 6. The schedule of assessments supplies timing details that must be reconciled with the governing protocol.
  4. principal investigator Turn 8. The principal investigator leads the study at the site and is part of the appropriate clarification route.
  5. protocol amendment Turn 10. A protocol amendment changes the study document and requires applicable authorization and implementation, not merely receipt by email.
  6. training record Turn 12. The training record helps establish whether the site team received the required instruction for an implemented change.
  7. protocol deviation Turn 14. A protocol deviation is a departure from the protocol; classification requires knowing which requirement actually applied.
  8. audit trail Turn 16. The audit trail preserves the history of recorded changes; silently altering dates would conceal rather than resolve the discrepancy.
  9. read-back Turn 18. A read-back repeats the key instruction and source, allowing misunderstanding to be detected before the team acts.
  10. essential records Turn 20. Essential records support reconstruction and evaluation of trial conduct, including the documented clarification relevant to this discrepancy.

Dialogue in the book, page 28 ↗
Three more conversations at work

Each short conversation has its own fictional situation and facts.

Which visit window controls?

Fictional trial coordination call: two documents describe different visit windows, and the controlling version is unconfirmed.

  1. Site coordinator: The visit guide and protocol give different windows. Which one should I communicate?
  2. Clinical monitor: Before answering, could you confirm the version identifiers on both documents?
  3. Site coordinator: I can read them back, but I haven't checked which version is controlling.
  4. Clinical monitor: Then let's verify that through document control instead of choosing the more convenient window.
  5. Site coordinator: The scheduling team wants an answer now. Can I call the difference a protocol deviation?
  6. Clinical monitor: Not from the discrepancy alone. First establish the applicable requirement and what actually happened.
  7. Site coordinator: I'll explain that the scheduling instruction is awaiting confirmation, without giving a replacement window.
  8. Clinical monitor: Please send the conflicting passages through the trial's authorized document channel.
  9. Site coordinator: Will you take ownership of checking the controlling version and returning a clear answer?
  10. Clinical monitor: Yes. I'll confirm the requirement with the responsible team and close the communication loop.
A consent discussion is not a completed consent record

Separate fictional training case: a tracker says consent discussed, while a meeting agenda says ready for randomization.

  1. Trial coordinator: Our agenda says ready for randomization, but the tracker only says consent discussed.
  2. Study nurse: That wording doesn't tell us whether the required informed consent process is complete.
  3. Trial coordinator: Could the two entries simply mean the same thing in different words?
  4. Study nurse: We need confirmation, not an assumption. Which authorized record supports the readiness status?
  5. Trial coordinator: I haven't checked it, and I don't have a verified completion entry.
  6. Study nurse: Then ask the responsible site clinician to confirm the status under the protocol.
  7. Trial coordinator: Should I change the agenda to consent status awaiting verification for now?
  8. Study nurse: Yes. That describes our knowledge without implying either completion or a confirmed failure.
  9. Trial coordinator: I'll also ask who updates the tracker once the status is verified.
  10. Study nurse: Good. We'll use the confirmed record for the next communication, not infer readiness from a heading.
Allocation wording in a recruitment briefing

Separate fictional recruitment rehearsal: a draft describes randomization as the coordinator choosing the most suitable study group.

  1. Recruitment coordinator: The briefing says I'll choose the most suitable group. Is that our randomization process?
  2. Trial educator: That wording sounds like personal selection. What does the approved protocol explanation say?
  3. Recruitment coordinator: It describes assignment through the study's randomization process, without a coordinator choosing.
  4. Trial educator: Then we should use that explanation and remove the suggestion of individual selection.
  5. Recruitment coordinator: Could I explain the exact allocation ratio to make the process clearer?
  6. Trial educator: Only after checking the approved information. We haven't established that ratio in this rehearsal.
  7. Recruitment coordinator: I'll ask which participant-facing wording is approved before the next practice session.
  8. Trial educator: Also distinguish explaining assignment from making promises about which group someone will enter.
  9. Recruitment coordinator: Understood. I'll clarify the process and refer questions beyond the materials to the study team.
  10. Trial educator: Let's rehearse that corrected explanation once the source wording has been confirmed.

F Say it

Two scenarios to practice

Two visit windows and no confirmed controlling version
  1. After checking the cloze key, read the scheduling call. Contrast the three-day and seven-day sources without selecting either as the controlling window.
  2. Switch roles for the clarification and read-back. Repeat the document identity, site-effective status, and exact window only when the script supplies confirmation.

On your own: read both roles. With a partner: swap roles after the first reading. Use the completed conversation to check any line you need to repeat.

Receipt does not establish applicability

A coordinator receives version 5 by email. The site record still identifies version 4 as effective. No implementation confirmation for version 5 has been supplied.

Choose one reply for each gap, then read the four turns in order. Check the explanation after each choice.

1. Coordinator: "Version 5 has been ___."

Answer and explanation

C. received

Email receipt is established, but the briefing supplies no confirmation of authorized implementation.

2. Monitor: "Its site applicability remains ___."

Answer and explanation

B. unconfirmed

The available record still names version 4, so applicability must be clarified.

3. Coordinator: "I will request implementation ___."

Answer and explanation

A. confirmation

The missing information concerns whether and when the newer version applies at the site.

4. Monitor: "Do not infer authority from file ___."

Answer and explanation

D. recency

A newer file alone does not establish the approval and effective status required to govern the work.

Read the completed exchange twice, switching roles. Keep the printed facts and professional responsibilities unchanged.

Build vocabulary and collocations — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Retrieve occupational vocabulary
1. Select four terms from the reference. Explain each in plain English, give two natural collocations and quote or create a short workplace example. Label invented examples. Contrast each term with a plausible confusable term; acknowledge regional variation.
2. Present one role-labelled exchange with one missing word or phrase and four choices A-D. Exactly one choice must fit the stated facts and grammar. Stop and wait for my answer before revealing it.
3. Explain all four options, then invite me to read the completed exchange aloud. Offer a sentence frame for optional spoken practice, never an open-ended writing assignment.
4. Repeat for the other three terms, one question at a time. Vary the correct letter and the situation; preserve the reference facts. If a choice is ambiguous, replace the item.
5. Finish with two new four-choice collocation questions for later review, with a clearly separate answer key. Do not claim to schedule a reminder.

Rehearse with an AI colleague — complete prompt

Copy the full text below into your preferred AI. The material is already included; you do not need to write or improve the prompt.

TASK: Interactive workplace role-play
1. Use the supplied case or dialogue as the starting situation. Give a two-sentence briefing and offer two relevant professional roles for me to choose from. For a supplied dialogue, use its actual roles. Ask which role I want, then stop and wait. Do not write my replies.
2. After I choose, identify who you will play and the immediate communication goal. Play the other professional; where a meeting requires a third person, label each of your speakers clearly. Start with one natural workplace turn and wait for my reply. Keep most turns to one to three sentences and ask no more than one question at a time.
3. Let the exchange develop across six to ten learner turns, or end earlier if I type "feedback". Respond to what I actually say. Include a plausible clarification, disagreement or tradeoff without silently changing the starting facts. Mark any added constraint as a fictional second-round variation. Do not resolve approvals, evidence or commitments that remain uncertain.
4. Stay in role during the exchange. If my meaning is unclear, ask for clarification naturally. Give a hint only if I ask or cannot proceed. Do not deliver a model conversation in advance.
5. At the debrief, quote two of my phrases: one successful choice and one worth improving. Check factual accuracy, language, register and whether the next step was clear. Give up to three focused suggestions. Ask me to retry the weakest turn; wait. Only then offer an alternative wording and a harder replay.
Use voice replies when available. If I prefer selections, offer four plausible spoken replies and explain my choice before continuing. Do not require written compositions.
